notes:
I've put together verse-by-verse notes on Revelation 5 below. Some things are missing. I found no Lutheran, Anglican, Orthodox, modern-scholarship (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org) or prosperity/word-of-faith material on this chapter, and verses 11–14 have thinner coverage than the rest. The clearest disagreements are on verse 8 (do the elders pray for us?), verses 9–10 ("us" or "them," and who the redemption is for) and verse 10 (when and how believers reign).

---

**v. 1: The sealed scroll**
- **Writing on both sides.** Guzik says scrolls weren't normally written on both sides, so this one held a great deal, nearly more than it could contain. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-5/
- **Ellicott** compares it with Ezekiel's scroll (Ezekiel 2:9–10): the writing that spills over shows the contents are complete, with "no room for addition." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/5.htm
- **Lying on the hand.** Ellicott reads the scroll as resting on the open palm of the hand, meaning God did not intend to keep it from anyone. https://biblehub.com/revelation/5-1.htm
- **The seven seals.** One scroll with seven seals on it, not seven separate writings. All the seals must be opened before the scroll could be read. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-5/
- **What is the scroll? Several views:**
  - *A will.* Guzik's preferred view: God's will, his final settlement of the universe's affairs. Under Roman law, wills were sealed seven times. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-5/ Carson (TGC) makes the same point with the emperor Vespasian, whose will took effect only when the right authorities broke its seven seals. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/revelation-5-en/
  - *A title deed.* Wiersbe calls it Christ's title deed to creation. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-5-commentary Chuck Smith links it to the sealed deed in Jeremiah 32. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/5-1.html Guzik finds this attractive but hard to prove, since God never "lost" the earth. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-5/
  - *A list of judgments.* Precept Austin says the seals hold all the judgments that will come on the earth as the Lamb takes dominion. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-5-commentary
  - *Older readings.* Victorinus thought it was the Old Testament. Bede said the inside writing was the New Testament and the back the Old. https://biblehub.com/revelation/5-1.htm
  - *Ellicott's broader view.* He thinks most of these readings are too narrow and calls it the book of God's government and salvation, which Christ alone can explain. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/5.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary** notes the book is never actually read in Revelation. It stands for the whole of God's mysteries, of which only a part is shown now. https://biblehub.com/revelation/5-1.htm
- **Wesley (Methodist)** says the right hand is the emblem of his all-ruling power. He also says there is no literal parchment book in heaven; the images point to real divine counsels. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/revelation/5.htm

**v. 2: The mighty angel's question**
- Guzik says nobody knows who the angel is; some suggest Gabriel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-5/
- Ellicott says "worthy" means moral fitness, not just strength. What stopped others from reading the book was moral unworthiness, not lack of intelligence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/5.htm

**v. 3: No one able**
- Guzik: creation cannot decide or bring about its own destiny. Only God can unfold this plan. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-5/
- Ellicott: "no one" covers more than humans. Being unable even to "look" may mean no one could bear the glory around the scroll. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/5.htm

**v. 4: John weeps**
- Guzik thinks John wept mainly because the end of history seemed to be put off indefinitely. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-5/
- Carson says John weeps because only God brings in the perfect world at the end of the age, and now there would be no final display of his mercy and judgment. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/revelation-5-en/
- Ellicott says the tears were not a failure of faith but a heart that cared deeply about God and people's destinies. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/5.htm

**v. 5: The Lion of Judah, the Root of David**
- **The titles.** "Lion of the tribe of Judah" comes from Genesis 49:9–10; "Root of David" from Isaiah 11:10. An elder, not an angel, comforts John. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-5/
- **"Triumphed."** Ellicott says the right to open rests on Christ's victory, not only on his being God's Son. As the Branch who is also the Root, he is both David's descendant and David's Lord. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/5.htm
- **Wesley:** he hath overcome all obstructions, and obtained the honour to disclose the divine counsels. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/revelation/5.htm

**v. 6: The slain Lamb**
- **Lion becomes Lamb.** John expects a Lion and sees a Lamb. Heaven's emblem is humility and sacrificial love, not a fierce beast. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-5/
- **A little lamb.** Ellicott notes the Greek word is a diminutive. It is the *suffering* Lamb that is exalted: alive and standing, but still bearing the wounds. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/5.htm
- **The sacrifice is still fresh.** Guzik (quoting Trapp and Clarke) says Christ's sacrifice remains current and effective before the Father. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-5/
- **Seven horns and seven eyes** mean complete power and complete knowledge. Ligonier: https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/the-lamb-takes-the-scroll and Wesley: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/revelation/5.htm
- **Who are the "seven Spirits"? Views differ:**
  - *The Holy Spirit.* This is the majority view. Ligonier calls it a metaphor for the fullness of the Holy Spirit: https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/the-lamb-takes-the-scroll Wesley says it is the Holy Ghost, called "seven" because of his manifold operations, not because there is more than one: https://www.ccel.org/ccel/wesley/notes.i.xxviii.ii.html
  - *Sent from the Son too.* Ellicott notes the Spirit belongs to the Son as well as the Father. "Sent" shares a root with "apostle," pointing to the Spirit's ongoing mission. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/5.htm
  - *Seven angels.* Constable and Gann suggest seven principal angels who report to Christ, and Clarke links the eyes with God's providence carried out through angels. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/5-6.html Bible.org allows this option but prefers the sevenfold Spirit. https://bible.org/seriespage/5-lamb-and-seven-sealed-book

**v. 7: He takes the scroll**
- Ellicott: the change of tense ("came," "has taken") shows how intensely John felt it. His weeping is over. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/5.htm
- Precept Austin, quoting another writer, says the Father won't break a single seal himself because he has given judgment to the Son (John 5:22–27). https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/63767/

**v. 8: Harps and golden bowls**
- **Harps.** Guzik: heaven's worship has music, and this verse is where the popular picture of harps in heaven comes from. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-5/
- **Prayer as incense.** Psalm 141:2 makes the link. Prayers are precious to God, like incense in golden bowls. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-5/
- **Spurgeon (Baptist)** says our prayers are fragrant to God only because of Christ's merit and because the Spirit inspires them. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons18.xxiv.html
- **A real disagreement: do the elders pray for us?**
  - *Catholic view.* The heavenly elders offer to God the prayers of the saints on earth, so they know of those prayers. https://www.catholic.com/tract/the-intercession-of-the-saints Another Catholic writer admits the verse doesn't explicitly tell us to ask saints to pray, but argues it can be inferred alongside other Scripture. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/intercession-of-the-saints-revealed
  - *Protestant replies.* Guzik says the elders present prayers but don't act as mediators, and the verse doesn't support praying to saints (1 Timothy 2:5). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-5/ GotQuestions notes the prayers belong to the saints rather than being addressed to them, and "saints" in Revelation means believers on earth. https://www.gotquestions.org/intercession-of-the-saints.html
  - *Spurgeon* doesn't object to saints in heaven praying. But he doubts this verse proves it, because by verse 13 the scene includes the whole universe. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons18.xxiv.html

**v. 9: The new song**
- **Why "new."** Poole (via Guzik) says it is new in content: Old Testament believers could not yet praise God for redemption actually accomplished. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-5/
- **"Worthy are You."** Guzik notes Roman emperors were greeted with *vere dignus* ("truly worthy"). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-5/
- **"Purchased."** Barnes says the Greek word means to buy, because redemption involved paying a price. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/revelation/5-9.html
- **"Us" or "them"?** Some manuscripts read "redeemed *us*"; most modern translations leave "us" out. https://bible.org/seriespage/revelation-4-5-0 Precept Austin argues there is good manuscript evidence for "us," and that the elders sing of their own redemption either way. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-5-commentary
- **For whom did Christ die?** This splits Calvinist and Arminian readers:
  - *Particular redemption (Calvinist).* Monergism finds it here: Christ purchased people *out of* every nation, a final exodus. https://www.monergism.com/reformation-theology/blog/particular-redemption-revelation-59 A Spurgeon sermon says heaven sings of not general redemption. It is particular redemption. https://biblehub.com/sermons/revelation/5-9.htm
  - *Wesleyan side.* I found no Wesleyan comment on this point.

**v. 10: A kingdom and priests who will reign**
- **Kingdom and priests.** This echoes Exodus 19:6. Monergism says believers are Israel fulfilled and expanded, not a replacement. https://www.monergism.com/reformation-theology/blog/particular-redemption-revelation-59
- **Text note.** Older manuscripts read "a kingdom," not "kings." They are also split between "they reign" and "they will reign." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/5-10.htm
- **When and how do believers reign? This is where millennial views divide:**
  - *Premillennial.* Precept Austin cites this verse for a literal 1,000-year earthly kingdom. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/revelation-topics-millennium Gill says it means more than a spiritual reign: the thousand-year reign on the new earth. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/amp/revelation/5-10.html
  - *Wesley (Methodist).* "Over the earth" means the new earth: after the first resurrection and into eternity. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/revelation-5.html
  - *Postmillennial-leaning.* Barnes reads it as true religion one day becoming dominant on earth, not saints ruling under a visible king. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/5-10.htm
  - *Spiritual reign now.* The Pulpit Commentary prefers "they reign" in the present tense: a spiritual reign over sin. It notes that your view of the millennium shapes how you read this verse. Alford (cited there) says the Church reigns even now, in the middle of persecution. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/revelation/5-10.htm

**v. 11: Countless angels**
- Wesley says the whole vision that follows is seen with the living creatures, elders, angels and all creatures watching the seals being opened. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/revelation/5.htm

**v. 12: Seven-fold praise**
- Precept Austin points out seven attributes given to the Lamb: "Worthy times seven!" https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-5-commentary
- Wesley says the angels speak of the Lamb in the third person ("Worthy is the Lamb") while the elders addressed him directly ("You are worthy"), because the elders were closer to him. He matches the seven-fold praise to the seven seals. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/revelation/5.htm

**v. 13: All creation joins in**
- Spurgeon reads this verse as showing the whole universe adoring the Lamb. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons18.xxiv.html
- Bible Hub's summary says the passage looks ahead to believers joining this chorus. https://biblehub.com/revelation/5.htm

**v. 14: "Amen" and worship**
- Bible Hub notes "amen" is a word of agreement, and *proskuneō* ("worship") means reverence and submission. https://biblehub.com/revelation/5.htm
